vignette:
He was forty-two when he drove the aid convoy into the eastern district. The ceasefire had held for nine days, and the local coordinator had assured him the route was clear. He remembers the dust, the way it coated the windshield even after the wipers ran dry. Ahead of him, a white van carrying medical supplies. Behind him, a truck with rice and lentils. He was the field director for a small non-governmental organization, and he had done this run a dozen times before.

The first crack came from the left. He thought it was a tire blowout. The second crack was closer, and he saw the driver of the white van slump forward. Then the world became noise—shattering glass, screaming, a man’s voice shouting in Arabic to reverse, reverse. He does not remember how he got out of the vehicle. He remembers crawling under the truck, the smell of diesel and hot metal, a woman’s hand gripping his arm, a child’s shoe on the ground. The shelling lasted maybe four minutes. When it stopped, three people were dead. He held a young boy’s head in his lap while a medic tried to stop the bleeding. The boy died before the helicopter arrived.

That was twenty-two years ago. Now he is a politician, a member of parliament in his adopted country, known for his measured speeches on foreign policy and humanitarian aid. His colleagues call him principled. His constituents call him tireless. But he has not slept more than three hours straight in two decades. At night, he lies awake and hears the cracks. Some mornings he finds himself on the bathroom floor, his back pressed against the wall, before he remembers where he is. He does not tell anyone. He cannot tell anyone.

During committee hearings, when the debate turns to military intervention, his hands sweat. He learned long ago to keep them below the table, to clench his fists until his nails press into his palms. The pain helps him stay present. He avoids footage of conflict zones on the evening news. If the coverage is unavoidable, he excuses himself to the restroom and stares at his reflection, counting breaths. His ex-wife once said he was not there, even when he was in the room. She meant his eyes—they would go flat, she said, like a curtain dropped. She left seven years ago. He does not blame her.

Yesterday, a young staffer brought him a briefing packet on a proposed humanitarian mission. The cover photo showed a destroyed school. He felt the familiar pressure behind his sternum, the heat climbing his neck. He put the packet in his desk drawer and did not open it. This morning, he found himself standing in the parking garage, staring at his car, unable to remember whether he had driven to work or taken the train. He stood there for ten minutes, keys in hand, until a security guard asked if he was all right. He said he was fine. He said it twice.

He does not speak of the boy whose head he held. He does not speak of the shoe. But he sees it, sometimes, in the corner of his vision—a small blue sneaker on the office carpet, on the sidewalk, on the floor of the grocery store. When he blinks, it is gone. He told me this only after three sessions, and his voice was flat, his eyes fixed on the wall behind me. He said, “I know it’s not real. But I look anyway.”
